messages.author: 10e1683268c0d540
messages.subject: Calculating landscape metrics in R
parts:
Dear D-RUGgies,

I am interested in using R to calculate some landscape metrics, similar to what I've used fragstats to do in the past (some examples of such metrics are here: 
http://www.umass.edu/landeco/teaching/landscape_ecology/schedule/chapter9_metrics.pdf). The landscapes of interests are circular buffers around my study sites.

I know there are a few R packages that can potentially do this. Some seem to be limited to binary landscapes (only two cover classes), though, and I am working with landscapes with multiple cover classes (and I want to use metrics that involve >2 cover classes, like interspersion).  

Also, some packages seem to require the landscape data be in a text-based raster, or at least some kind of raster. I can convert to raster if necessary (although I'm not sure how to convert to a text raster), but my landscape cover data is in polygons right now, and I'm wondering if there's any way to analyze it without converting it. 

Not sure if this is possible exactly as described, so I'd appreciate any suggestions for reasonable ways to go about it! I'm open to other approaches besides R too. Fragstats seemed pretty clunky last time I used it so I'm hoping to avoid it if possible.

Thanks much,
Jesse


Jesse E. D. Miller
Botanist - Ecologist
Postdoctoral Researcher
Department of Environmental Science and Policy
University of California-Davis
http://jesseedmiller.com

messages.author: 5f533b50135a7f86
messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: Calculating landscape metrics in R
parts:
Hi Jesse, 

There are a couple of different sets of packages to work with spatial data in R.  I think I recently did something like what you’re trying to do using the sf package, which is designed to work with the tidyverse packages (dplyr, etc).  IIRC the raster package is used to construct buffers with the Spatial*DataFrame classes, even when * = Polygons.  

Do you already have your data loaded into R?  If so, can you generate a sample dataset?  Knowing the classes you’re working with and how your data are structured would make answering your question much easier.  

Dan

Hi Jesse,

If this is the first time you've done spatial R stuff, I highly recommend this resource as a place to get started and be reminded of how to do some useful things   http://www.rspatial.org/ and the raster package in general.  These resources will help you get your data (shapefile?)  into a R working environment.

Based on the landscape metrics link you shared, it looks like you'll need some even more specialized R package to do your calculations, unless you want to write your own functions.  Looks like SDMTools may have some of what you need, specifically the function PatchStat ???

Scott

parts: Also since you’re specifically looking at fire severity, Mike Koontz (Andrew Latimer’s lab) and Zack Steel (Safford lab) have both done work with fire severity spatial analyses of different types.
On Jul 14, 2018, at 11:13 AM, Jan Ng <jn...@ucdavis.edu> wrote:

Hi Jesse,

If you haven't yet, maybe consider asking Robert Hijmans (GGE prof who co-authored the R raster package) or Michele Tobias (the geospatial consultant for the DSI on campus, she not only knows a ton about spatial analysis but is a good point person for finding other specialists on campus). Also, Elise Hellwig (GGE student in the Hijmans lab) has done spatial analysis stuff in R as well.

Cheers!

Jan

Cheers,
Jesse

On Fri, Jul 13, 2018 at 12:16 PM, Daniel Hicks <hicks.d...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi Jesse, 

Sorry I haven’t been able to follow up with this.  I’m leaving on a weeklong vacation tomorrow, so I won’t be able to help in a timely manner.  If you haven’t started looking into it already, this sf vignette illustrates how to load shapefiles:  
https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/sf/vignettes/sf2.html

`sf::st_buffer()` is used to construct buffers, and `sf::st_join()` does spatial joins.  Hopefully that’s enough to get you started!  

Dan

On Wed, Jul 11, 2018 at 2:25 PM, Daniel Hicks <hicks.d...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hi Jesse, 

There are a couple of different sets of packages to work with spatial data in R.  I think I recently did something like what you’re trying to do using the sf package, which is designed to work with the tidyverse packages (dplyr, etc).  IIRC the raster package is used to construct buffers with the Spatial*DataFrame classes, even when * = Polygons.  

Do you already have your data loaded into R?  If so, can you generate a sample dataset?  Knowing the classes you’re working with and how your data are structured would make answering your question much easier.  

Dan

On Jul 11, 2018, at 12:58 PM, Jesse Miller <jedm...@ucdavis.edu> wrote:


Dear D-RUGgies,

I am interested in using R to calculate some landscape metrics, similar to what I've used fragstats to do in the past (some examples of such metrics are here: 
http://www.umass.edu/landeco/teaching/landscape_ecology/schedule/chapter9_metrics.pdf). The landscapes of interests are circular buffers around my study sites.

I know there are a few R packages that can potentially do this. Some seem to be limited to binary landscapes (only two cover classes), though, and I am working with landscapes with multiple cover classes (and I want to use metrics that involve >2 cover classes, like interspersion).  

Also, some packages seem to require the landscape data be in a text-based raster, or at least some kind of raster. I can convert to raster if necessary (although I'm not sure how to convert to a text raster), but my landscape cover data is in polygons right now, and I'm wondering if there's any way to analyze it without converting it. 

Not sure if this is possible exactly as described, so I'd appreciate any suggestions for reasonable ways to go about it! I'm open to other approaches besides R too. Fragstats seemed pretty clunky last time I used it so I'm hoping to avoid it if possible.

Thanks much,
Jesse
